get_instance_status.label: Checking status
get_instance_status.description: Reports one instance's current state: whether it is running, its game and process, its version and whether an update is available, its configured ports and whether the host firewall has them open and the router forwards them, its disk use, and how many backups it has. Answers whether a server is up, and whether anyone outside can reach it. Name the instance. Leaving instance_name out answers one question only — "what's running?", across the whole host — and answers nothing about any single server. Which instances exist and what game each runs is in the list above already.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The instance to report on. Give it whenever the question is about a server. Leave it out only for a question about the whole host at once.

get_instance_config.label: Reading config
get_instance_config.description: Lists every KGSM setting for one instance with its current value, and says which of them can be changed. The keys it reports are the keys set_instance_kgsm_setting takes, so a value read here can be changed by passing the same key back. These are KGSM's settings for the server (auto-update, backup schedule, memory cap, restart schedule, launch arguments); read_instance_file shows the game's own configuration file instead.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The instance whose settings to report.

get_instance_version.label: Checking version
get_instance_version.description: Reports the version one instance currently has installed and whether an update is available. This is the instance's own installed version; search_documentation_and_web covers what the game's developers have published. get_event_history covers when it was last updated.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The instance whose version to report.

list_online_players.label: Checking who is online
list_online_players.description: Lists who is connected right now. With no instance_name it covers every instance at once. It reports live presence; moderate_player acts on a player, and get_event_history covers who joined or left earlier.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: One instance to report on. Omitted, the report covers every instance at once, which answers a question about the whole fleet in a single call.

list_instance_backups.label: Listing backups
list_instance_backups.description: Lists the backups one instance has, newest first. Each carries the id manage_instance_backups takes, how long ago it was taken, the game version it captured, its size, and which of the server's directories it actually holds — which is what decides whether restoring it brings back the world. Leaving instance_name out answers for EVERY server in one call, saying how long ago each was last backed up — that is the answer to "does anything need a backup?" or "when was everything last backed up?", so ask it that way once instead of asking server by server. Name the instance for a question about one server, or when you need its individual backup ids. Creating a new backup is a lifecycle action and lives on control_instance.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The instance whose backups to list. Leave it out for a question about every server's backups at once.

get_instance_note.label: Reading the note
get_instance_note.description: Reports the server note attached to one instance — free text a person left about it, with who wrote it and when. It reports whether a note is set, so an instance with none is answered as having none.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The instance whose note to report.

get_instance_autostart.label: Checking autostart
get_instance_autostart.description: Reports whether an instance starts when the host boots. With no instance_name it covers every instance at once. Starting an instance now is control_instance with verb=start; changing this setting is control_instance with verb=enable_autostart or disable_autostart.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: One instance to report on. Omitted, the report covers every instance at once, which answers a question about the whole fleet in a single call.

get_host_vitals.label: Checking host health
get_host_vitals.description: Reports on the host machine the instances run on, rather than on any one instance: its uptime, load, memory, disk space, external IP address and whether a reboot is pending. get_instance_resource_usage covers what one instance is using.

list_host_ports.label: Reading host ports
list_host_ports.description: Lists every port the host is listening on right now, split into the ones a game server is configured for — naming which server — and the ones nothing here owns. It reports the whole machine. One instance's own ports and whether they are open come back from get_instance_status.

find_port_conflicts.label: Looking for port conflicts
find_port_conflicts.description: Reports whether any two claimants want the same port: two instances configured for one port, or an instance whose port a process outside KGSM already holds. It compares what they are configured to use, which is how a conflict is found before both are running.

get_blueprint_info.label: Reading the game catalog
get_blueprint_info.description: Reports on blueprints — the game types that can be installed. With no blueprint_name it lists every blueprint. With one it describes that game type: the ports it needs, its resource requirements, and what it supports. A blueprint is a recipe, so this reports what a game type would need, never the state of anything running; get_instance_status reports on an instance that is installed.

params.name: blueprint_name
params.description: One blueprint to describe in detail — the ports it needs, its resource needs, and what it supports — by the name it is listed under. Omitted, it lists every game type that can be installed.

get_event_history.label: Reading recent events
get_event_history.description: The whole history of what has happened, read from KGSM's own event log, most recent first. Covers one instance with instance_name, or every instance without one. One unfiltered timeline: starts, stops, restarts, crashes, installs, updates, version changes, backups, port changes and player activity all arrive together, and what answers the question is read off it. This is the record of what happened to this host's own instances — when one was updated, restarted, backed up or crashed. read_instance_console gives what a server itself printed, which is a separate record.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: One instance to scope the get_event_history to. Omitted, the feed covers every instance on this host, which answers a question about the fleet in a single call.

params.name: window
params.description: How far back to look. Defaults to 24h.

check_instance_health.label: Running health check
check_instance_health.description: A health check on one instance, returned as a ranked summary. It combines four readings in a single call: whether the instance is running, errors in its recent logs, whether an update is available, and host disk space. It describes the present; diagnose_instance_failure investigates an incident in the past.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

get_instance_resource_usage.label: Reading metrics
get_instance_resource_usage.description: One instance's resource usage: CPU as a percentage of one core, memory, network and disk-I/O throughput, and process count. With no range it is a live snapshot of current values. With a range it is the trend across that window. A running instance has both. A stopped instance has no live snapshot, and may still have recent history. This covers one instance; host_info covers the machine they all run on.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: range
params.description: Optional. OMIT for a live snapshot of current usage. Provide a time window to get the TREND over that period instead (a chart of how CPU/memory changed) — use this for "how has X been doing over the last hour/day?", "is X's memory climbing?", "CPU trend for X".

diagnose_instance_failure.label: Tracing the root cause
diagnose_instance_failure.description: Investigates why one instance crashed, will not stay up, or has been misbehaving. It gathers the instance's event history, resource usage and health checks in a single call and matches them against known failure patterns — port conflicts, update-triggered crash loops, disk-full failures, mismatches between the event log and live state — then returns a ranked explanation with the evidence behind it. It covers an incident in the past; check_instance_health covers the present. When no known pattern matches, it reports the correlation it found.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: range
params.description: Optional. How far back to look for evidence. Defaults to 24h if omitted.

search_documentation_and_web.label: Searching docs & web
search_documentation_and_web.description: Looks a topic up and returns short passages, each with its source — a doc path or a URL. It reads the operator's indexed documentation and the public web. It covers facts about a game or a piece of software that hold anywhere: what its settings do, what its release notes say, which version its developers have published. Facts about this host's own instances are measured directly by the KGSM tools instead — which version an instance has installed and whether an update is available come from get_instance_version, and when an instance was last updated, restarted or backed up comes from get_event_history. A passage can be out of date, so it is worth citing its source and saying so.

params.name: query
params.description: The topic to look up. It covers facts about a game or a piece of software that hold anywhere — what a config option means, what a release note says, which version the developers have published. Facts about this host's own instances (status, config, health, which version is installed, when it was last updated) are measured directly by get_instance_status and get_event_history instead.

params.name: scope
params.description: Where to look. web: the public web only, which is the source for anything that changes over time — a current version, a release date, recent news — and for anything the user asks you to check online. local: the operator's own documentation only. auto (the default): the documentation first, then the web when nothing there scores well enough. A local guide about a game matches a question about that game whether or not it addresses what was asked, so an auto result can be about the right game and silent on the question; the same words with scope=web ask a different source.

read_web_page.label: Reading a web page
read_web_page.description: Reads the full text of one web page by its exact URL — an official docs page, a Steam store page, a raw GitHub file. It takes a URL you already have, from the user or from a search_documentation_and_web result. search_documentation_and_web is what finds a page by topic and returns short summaries; this reads one page you can already name. Public http/https pages only, and a large page is truncated.

params.name: url
params.description: The exact web address to read, including scheme — e.g. an official server-setup doc, a Steam store page, or a raw Dockerfile URL. Only public http/https pages can be fetched.

read_instance_file.label: Reading a file
read_instance_file.description: Reads a text file inside one instance's own directory — the game's configuration, its logs, server.properties, a mod's settings. Read-only, and confined to that instance's folder. The path is relative to the instance's directory; omitting it reads the instance's KGSM configuration (its .config.ini). Large files are truncated and binary files are not shown. A change to a game's own config file is proposed with edit_instance_file; a change to the .config.ini is proposed with set_instance_kgsm_setting.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: path
params.description: The file to read, as a path relative to the instance's own directory — server.properties, logs/latest.log. Omitted, it reads the instance's KGSM configuration (its .config.ini). find_instance_file locates a file by name and search_instance_files locates one by its contents.

list_instance_directory.label: Listing files
list_instance_directory.description: Lists the files and folders inside one instance's own directory, one level at a time, with each one's size and when it was last changed. It answers what is in a directory, and which of the things in it was touched recently. find_instance_file searches every subdirectory for a file by name, and search_instance_files searches inside every file for text.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: subdir
params.description: Optional. A subdirectory to list, relative to the server's own directory — e.g. "logs" or "install". OMIT it to list the server's top level.

find_instance_file.label: Finding a file
find_instance_file.description: Finds a file anywhere inside one instance's folder by name, searching every subdirectory in a single call. A game's own config often sits several directories deep, so one glob reaches it where stepping down a level at a time takes many calls. It returns matching paths ready to pass to read_instance_file. Archived copies under a backups folder are excluded, so what comes back is the live file.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: pattern
params.description: The file name as a glob — PalWorldSettings.ini, *.ini, server.properties, *Settings*. A / in the pattern matches against the path rather than the name, e.g. */Config/*.ini. The most specific pattern that fits returns the fewest files; a broad one can match hundreds.

params.name: subdir
params.description: Optional. Search only inside this subdirectory of the server's folder. OMIT it to search_documentation_and_web the whole server directory, which is usually what you want.

search_instance_files.label: Searching in files
search_instance_files.description: Searches inside one instance's files for text, across every subdirectory in a single call. It finds which file holds a setting when the setting's name is known and the file's is not — MaxPlayers, DayTimeSpeedRate. It returns each matching file with the line number and the line itself, ready to pass to read_instance_file. find_instance_file searches by file name instead. Archived copies under a backups folder are excluded, and binary files are skipped.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: text
params.description: The text to look for inside the files — a setting name such as MaxPlayers or DayTimeSpeedRate. Matching ignores case and a regular expression works. This is file content rather than a file name, so it takes the bare text with no * around it. A distinctive string returns the fewest lines; a common word can match hundreds.

params.name: subdir
params.description: Optional. Search only inside this subdirectory of the server's folder. OMIT it to search_documentation_and_web the whole server directory, which is usually what you want.

read_instance_console.label: Reading console output
read_instance_console.description: Reads what an instance itself printed — its console output. It covers what an instance is saying now, and what it said on its way down; a stopped instance's last output is still readable. get_event_history covers KGSM's own record of what happened to the instance, which is a separate record from what the game printed. The reply names which run it came from and whether the instance restarted recently. An instance's log restarts from empty every time it starts, so after a crash-restart the crash is in run 1 and run 0 holds the clean boot that followed it.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: lines
params.description: Optional. How many of the most recent console lines to read. Defaults to a recent tail.

params.name: run
params.description: Optional. Which run of the server to read, newest first: 0 is the current run (the default), 1 the run before it, and so on. A server's log restarts from empty every time it starts, so after a crash-restart the crash is in run 1 while run 0 holds only the clean boot that followed it.

control_instance.label: Running command
control_instance.description: Proposes a lifecycle action on one existing instance, chosen with the 'verb' parameter. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: verb
params.description: Which action to take. start: run a stopped instance now. stop: stop a running one. restart: stop it and start it again. update: bring it to its latest version. backup: take one now. enable_autostart and disable_autostart: whether it starts when the host boots. start acts now, and enable_autostart acts at the next boot.

manage_instance_backups.label: Managing backups
manage_instance_backups.description: Acts on the backups an instance already has: restore one, delete one, or prune the old ones. Name which backup with "newest" or "oldest" — those need no id. An id from list_instance_backups also works. Creating a new backup is a lifecycle action and lives on control_instance.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: verb
params.description: What to do with the instance's existing backups. delete: remove exactly one backup, the one named in backup_name — this is what removes a single backup, however that one is described. prune: remove SEVERAL at once, the oldest ones, keeping the most recent few; it takes no backup_name because it does not act on one. restore: replace the instance's current data with a backup. list_instance_backups shows them oldest to newest with the ids delete takes. control_instance with verb=backup creates a new one.

params.name: backup_name
params.description: Which backup to act on, for restore and delete. "newest" or "oldest" names it by position and is what a request like "the most recent backup" means. A full id from list_instance_backups also works. Not used by prune, which takes 'keep' instead.

params.name: keep
params.description: For prune only: how many of the most recent backups to keep. Omit for the server's configured retention.

moderate_player.label: Moderating a player
moderate_player.description: Proposes moderating a player on one instance: kick, ban, or unban them. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms. Moderation works on games whose server supports moderation commands, and the tool reports when a game does not.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: verb
params.description: What to do with the player: kick (disconnect them now), ban (disconnect and block them), or unban (lift a ban).

params.name: target
params.description: Which player, exactly as the user named them. list_online_players lists who is connected. The game decides which form of identifier it needs and the system supplies it, so the name as the user gave it is the right thing to pass.

install_instance.label: Installing a server
install_instance.description: Proposes installing a new instance from a blueprint. The blueprint is the game type; the instance is the server this creates from it. Heavy and slow. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms.

params.name: blueprint_name
params.description: The blueprint to install, by the name it is listed under, e.g. "Project Zomboid".

params.name: instance_name
params.description: Optional custom name for the new instance. Omit to let the system name it.

params.name: version
params.description: Optional. A specific version to install. Omit for the latest, which is almost always right.

params.name: port
params.description: Optional. Override the blueprint's primary game port. Omit unless the user asked for a specific port or a conflict needs avoiding.

params.name: library
params.description: Optional. The library — the disk the new server's files go on — by the name the user gave for it. Pass it ONLY when the user named one; omit it otherwise and the host puts the server on its usual disk. Never guess a name: the libraries this host has are not listed here, so an invented one is refused when the install is confirmed.

uninstall_instance.label: Uninstalling a server
uninstall_instance.description: Proposes permanently deleting one instance and all of its data. Irreversible. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

set_instance_kgsm_setting.label: Changing a KGSM setting
set_instance_kgsm_setting.description: Proposes setting one key=value in an instance's KGSM configuration (its .config.ini) — settings such as auto_update, executable_arguments, or a timeout. A change to the game's own config file is proposed with set_instance_game_setting (one Key=Value setting) or edit_instance_file (any other edit) instead. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms. kgsm keeps identity and structural keys, path keys (*_dir and *_file), ports, and the integration toggles (enable_firewall_management, enable_port_forwarding, enable_command_shortcuts) to their own dedicated flows, so one of those is rejected at confirmation time and the tool says which.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: config_key
params.description: The configuration key to set, e.g. "auto_update", "executable_arguments", or "stop_command_timeout_seconds".

params.name: config_value
params.description: The new value for the key. Pass an empty string to clear the setting.

edit_instance_file.label: Editing a file
edit_instance_file.description: Proposes a change to a text file inside one instance's own directory — the game's own config file, such as Palworld's PalWorldSettings.ini, server.properties, or a mod's settings file. It takes only the text that changes: old_string is the exact text to replace, copied from read_instance_file's output, and new_string is what it becomes. The rest of the file is preserved byte for byte. old_string has to match exactly once; a match in no place, or in several, stages nothing and returns an error saying which, and reading the file again for the exact text resolves it. set_instance_game_setting changes one Key=Value setting by naming its key, which needs no copied text and is the way to change a setting in a config that packs every setting onto one line; KGSM's own settings (ports, launch arguments, auto-update) are proposed with set_instance_kgsm_setting. Staged for human confirmation against a preview: it does not run until a person confirms, and a running instance picks the change up on its next restart.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: path
params.description: The file to change, as a path relative to the instance's own directory — install/Pal/Saved/Config/LinuxServer/PalWorldSettings.ini, server.properties. find_instance_file locates it by name and read_instance_file shows its contents.

params.name: old_string
params.description: The exact text to replace, copied character for character from what read_instance_file showed you — normally the one setting being changed, e.g. "Difficulty=None". It has to appear exactly once in the file; where it appears more than once, a little of the surrounding text narrows it to one place. Everything else in the file is preserved for you.

params.name: new_string
params.description: What that text becomes, e.g. "Difficulty=Difficulty_Hard". To add a setting, put a nearby existing line in old_string and that same line plus the new one here. An empty value deletes the old text.

params.name: copy_from
params.description: For a file that is empty or does not exist yet, when the game ships a default or reference file beside it (e.g. "install/DefaultPalWorldSettings.ini"): its content is copied into the file server-side and the old_string/new_string replacement is applied to that copy. Left out when editing a file that already has content.

create_blueprint.label: Setting up a new game
create_blueprint.description: Authors a blueprint for a game that is missing from the catalog. It runs its own online research and drafts a server config in a single call, then shows the draft to the user in an editor to review and tweak. Calling it is what starts the research and the drafting, so it is the whole first step and needs no search_documentation_and_web, read_web_page or get_blueprint_info call ahead of it. The test-install and verification run later, when the user saves the config, so that is the point at which the game is added. get_blueprint_info lists the games already in the catalog, and a game already there is installed with install_instance. Not every game can be self-hosted or has a native Linux server, and the tool reports either outcome.

params.name: game
params.description: The game to add, by its common name — "Terraria", "Rust". A blueprint slug is not what this takes.

revise_blueprint.label: Updating the draft
revise_blueprint.description: Updates the blueprint draft the user is currently reviewing in the editor — a metadata field (min or recommended RAM, max players, disk), a port, the launch args, any part of it. The draft's current YAML is given in this turn's context; revised_yaml takes that whole document with the requested change applied. It re-validates and shows the updated draft to review and save, and installs nothing. This tool is what changes an open draft, and the change is real once it returns successfully.

params.name: revised_yaml
params.description: The complete updated blueprint YAML: the whole document, being the open draft's current content with the requested change applied. It is the full document rather than a fragment or a diff, and every field the user did not ask about keeps its current value.

set_instance_game_setting.label: Changing a game setting
set_instance_game_setting.description: Proposes changing one Key=Value setting in a game's own config file, naming the setting by its key. The value currently on disk is read here, so only the key and the new value are sent and the rest of the file is preserved byte for byte. This works whichever shape the config has — one setting per line, or every setting packed onto a single line, which is where naming the surrounding text stops being possible. The reply names the value that was there before. edit_instance_file covers a change that is not one setting's value, such as adding a line or editing prose; set_instance_kgsm_setting covers KGSM's own settings rather than the game's. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms, and a running instance picks the change up on its next restart.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: path
params.description: The game's own config file. Its NAME is enough — "PalWorldSettings.ini", "server.properties" — and it is looked up under the instance, so the directories around it do not have to be right. A full path works too. When the name matches several files, the reply lists them and a full path picks one; search_instance_files finds the file that carries a given setting.

params.name: setting
params.description: The setting's key on its own, without an '=' or the rest of the line — "DayTimeSpeedRate", "Difficulty", "max-players". Case does not have to match the file. The key has to be set exactly once in the file; a key set in two places is reported rather than guessed at.

params.name: value
params.description: The value the setting becomes, written exactly as the file spells values — "0.500000", "Difficulty_Hard", "20". Quotes are part of the value where the file quotes it. An empty string clears the value and keeps the setting.

params.name: copy_from
params.description: For a config that is empty or does not exist yet, when the game ships a default or reference file beside it (e.g. "install/DefaultPalWorldSettings.ini"): its content is copied in server-side and the setting changed on that copy. Left out when editing a file that already has content.

remember.label: Writing it down
remember.description:
Writes one thing down about the person you are talking to, so later conversations start already knowing it. Use it for what stays true after this conversation ends: how they like things done, a standing instruction, what they call something, a correction to something you got wrong, or a decision they want kept to. Say what you wrote down.

REFUSE to write down any value a tool can read. Before calling this, ask whether some tool reports the thing: a port, a version, a player count, free disk, an address, whether a server is running. If one does, this is the WRONG tool — do not call it, even when the person states the value as a fact and even when they say it specifically so you will know it. Such a value changes with no one telling you, and repeating it later is a confident wrong answer. Reply that you will check it with a tool whenever it matters, and write nothing down.

Do not write down what was said in passing, what you can look up, or anything the person did not mean to be kept.

params.name: key
params.description: A short name for this memory, in lowercase words joined by hyphens, like 'preferred-test-game'. Writing again under a key that already exists REPLACES it — that is how you correct a memory.

params.name: summary
params.description: The one line you will be shown at the start of every later conversation. State the fact itself — 'Tests new servers with Factorio' — never that a note exists.

params.name: body
params.description: Any detail worth keeping that does not fit the summary, read only when you ask for this memory by name. Leave it out when the summary says everything.

forget.label: Forgetting it
forget.description: Drops one thing you remember about this person, by its key. Use it when they ask you to forget something, or when they tell you something that makes a memory wrong and there is nothing to replace it with — if there IS a replacement, write the new one under the same key instead.

params.name: key
params.description: The key of the memory to drop, as shown in what you remember about this person.

recall.label: Recalling
recall.description: Reads one of your memories about this person in full. You are already shown a one-line summary of every one of them at the start of the conversation — use this only when a summary points at detail you need and do not have. It tells you nothing about any server.

params.name: key
params.description: The key of the memory to read in full.
